    Platelets — number and function are different

    1Adhesion

    vWF links platelet to damaged vessel wall.

    →
    2Activation

    Shape change + granule release.

    →
    3Aggregation

    Platelet plug forms.

    Platelet-type bleeding

    Petechiae, mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, gingival bleeding — though patterns overlap.

    Drug effect

    Aspirin/P2Y12 inhibitors impair function even when count is normal.

    vWD

    Common inherited bleeding disorder affects adhesion and factor VIII biology.

    Count trend

    Rate/timing of fall often matters more than one isolated platelet value.

    HEME 03 • SECONDARY HEMOSTASIS

    Coagulation Labs — what is the test actually sampling?

    PT / INR

    Sensitive to vitamin K-dependent/extrinsic-common pathway effects; used to monitor warfarin. INR is not a universal bleeding-risk meter.

    aPTT

    Intrinsic/common pathway screen; used for some UFH protocols but affected by multiple conditions.

    Fibrinogen

    Substrate converted to fibrin. Can fall in consumption/massive bleeding; can rise as acute-phase reactant.

    D-dimer

    Fibrin breakdown marker — sensitive in some VTE/DIC contexts but nonspecific in illness, surgery, inflammation and age.

    Never ask “is the INR high?” alone. Ask why: warfarin? liver disease? vitamin K deficiency? DIC? lab artifact? And is the patient bleeding or thrombosing?
    HEME 04 • ANTICOAGULATION

    Anticoagulants — clot prevention with bleeding trade-off

    UFH

    Rapid onset/offset; aPTT or anti-Xa depending protocol. Protamine reversal concept.

    LMWH

    More predictable; renal clearance matters. Protamine only partially reverses activity.

    Warfarin

    Vitamin K antagonist; monitor INR. Major bleeding reversal commonly uses 4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K.

    Dabigatran

    Direct thrombin inhibitor; renal function important. Idarucizumab is specific reversal.

    Factor Xa DOACs

    Apixaban/rivaroxaban etc.; renal/hepatic function and timing of last dose matter. Andexanet alfa or PCC pathways depend on indication/protocol.

    Antiplatelet ≠ anticoagulant

    Aspirin/clopidogrel target platelets, not coagulation factors.

    HEME 05 • LOW PLATELETS

    Thrombocytopenia — five buckets

    Production ↓

    Marrow failure/suppression, infection, drugs, B12/folate.

    Destruction ↑

    Immune ITP, drug-induced mechanisms.

    Consumption

    DIC, TMA, major bleeding.

    Sequestration

    Splenomegaly/portal hypertension.

    Dilution / artifact

    Massive transfusion or EDTA clumping/pseudothrombocytopenia.

    Ask first: Is it real? How fast did it fall? Is there thrombosis? Is there hemolysis? Is the patient septic? Was heparin started? Is there splenomegaly?
    HEME 06 • DIC

    DIC — clotting everywhere, bleeding because the system is consumed

    Triggersepsis • trauma • malignancy • obstetric etc.
    →
    Coagulation activation
    →
    Microthrombi
    +
    Platelet/factor consumption

    Typical lab pattern

    Platelets ↓, PT/aPTT may prolong, fibrinogen can fall, D-dimer/fibrin degradation products rise — pattern varies with stage/cause.

    Clinical

    Bleeding from lines/wounds, ecchymoses, organ ischemia/failure, thrombosis.

    Priority

    Treat the trigger/source. Blood products are guided by bleeding/procedure/lab context, not “normalize every number”.

    Trend

    Serial platelets, PT, fibrinogen and clinical organ status matter.

    HEME 07 • HIT

    HIT — low platelets, high thrombosis risk

    1Suspect pattern

    Platelet fall/timing + thrombosis + other causes.

    →
    24Ts

    Estimate pretest probability.

    →
    3If intermediate/high

    Stop heparin, start appropriate non-heparin anticoagulant, send testing.

    ASH: do not send HIT testing or empirically stop heparin/start alternate anticoagulant for a clearly low 4Ts probability unless key information is uncertain. HIT is prothrombotic — platelet transfusion is not the reflex treatment.
    HEME 08 • PRODUCTS

    Blood Products — replace the missing component

    RBC

    Raises oxygen-carrying red cell mass; does not replace platelets or coagulation factors.

    Platelets

    Increase platelet number/function capacity; indication depends on bleeding/procedure/count/cause.

    Plasma

    Contains multiple coagulation factors; use for specific factor-deficiency/coagulopathy indications, not simple volume expansion.

    Cryoprecipitate

    Fibrinogen-rich product (also factor VIII, XIII, vWF/fibronectin); used mainly when fibrinogen replacement is needed.

    AABB 2023: for most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, restrictive RBC transfusion is considered around Hb <7 g/dL, with individualized higher thresholds in selected groups/clinical contexts.
    HEME 09 • REACTIONS

    Transfusion Reaction — stop first, investigate second

    Acute hemolytic

    Fever/chills, pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria/DIC; compatibility error is a critical concern.

    Febrile nonhemolytic

    Fever/chills without hemolysis after serious causes excluded.

    Allergic/anaphylaxis

    Urticaria to airway/shock.

    TACO

    Circulatory overload: dyspnea, hypertension, pulmonary edema/volume signs.

    TRALI

    Acute hypoxemic noncardiogenic pulmonary edema temporally associated with transfusion.

    Septic reaction

    High fever/rigors, hypotension; bacterial contamination requires urgent sepsis/blood-bank pathway.

    AABB transfusion safety principle: at the first sign of a suspected reaction, stop the transfusion, keep appropriate IV access per protocol, recheck patient/product identification, assess ABC/vitals and notify the blood bank/medical team for directed workup.
    HEME 10 • CHALLENGE

    Hematology אתגר יסודות

    Platelets fall 220→85 on day 7 of heparin + new DVT.

    Think HIT; calculate 4Ts and use HIT pathway, not “just transfuse platelets”.

    Septic shock + platelets 40 + INR 2.0 + fibrinogen falling + oozing.

    DIC pattern; treat sepsis/source while supporting hemostasis based on bleeding and labs.

    Hb 6.7, stable inpatient, no active bleeding.

    Restrictive transfusion consideration around 7 g/dL, integrated with symptoms/comorbidity.

    10 min after RBC starts: fever, back pain, hypotension.

    Stop transfusion immediately and activate reaction workup.

    Normal platelet count on aspirin, mucosal bleeding.

    Platelet function can be impaired despite normal count.

    HEME 11 • HEMOLYSIS

    Hemolysis Lab — is the RBC being destroyed?

    אל תסתפק ב-Hb נמוך. חפש חתימה של destruction.

    Reticulocytes ↑

    Marrow response to RBC loss/destruction — unless marrow reserve is impaired.

    LDH ↑

    Cell breakdown marker; supports hemolysis but is not specific alone.

    Indirect bilirubin ↑

    Heme breakdown can raise unconjugated bilirubin.

    Haptoglobin ↓

    Especially supportive of intravascular hemolysis because free Hb consumes haptoglobin.

    Smear

    Schistocytes suggest mechanical/microangiopathic fragmentation; spherocytes suggest other mechanisms.

    Urine / kidneys

    Hemoglobinuria and AKI can occur in substantial intravascular hemolysis.

    Mental model: anemia + reticulocytosis + LDH↑ + indirect bilirubin↑ + haptoglobin↓ = hemolysis pattern. Then ask why: immune, mechanical, microangiopathic, inherited, drug/toxin, infection.
    HEME 12 • TMA

    TMA / TTP / HUS — microthrombi can destroy RBCs and organs

    Endothelial / VWF problem→Platelet-rich microthrombi→Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia→Brain / kidney / heart injury

    TTP pattern

    MAHA + thrombocytopenia with variable neurologic, renal, cardiac and systemic findings. Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency supports immune TTP.

    Why time matters

    Suspected immune TTP is a hematologic emergency. Do not wait for the historical “pentad” or for every confirmatory result before specialist-directed treatment pathway.

    Current treatment concept

    Therapeutic plasma exchange + corticosteroid-based immunosuppression, with caplacizumab/rituximab in contemporary iTTP pathways according to specialist protocol.

    Different from DIC

    TTP often has relatively preserved routine coagulation tests compared with consumptive DIC; context and full lab pattern are essential.

    Bedside red flag: platelets low + new confusion/focal symptoms + hemolysis/schistocytes = escalate urgently. Platelet transfusion is generally not a reflex intervention in TTP without compelling bleeding indication.
    HEME 13 • ITP

    ITP — isolated platelet problem until proven otherwise

    Typical pattern

    Isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise compatible CBC/smear and no better alternative explanation. Mucocutaneous bleeding is common.

    What changes urgency

    Active major bleeding, very low platelets, anticoagulants, trauma/procedure, intracranial symptoms, pregnancy and comorbidity.

    Treatment logic: observation can be appropriate in selected adults with higher counts and little/no bleeding; when treatment is required, corticosteroids and/or IVIG are common first-line concepts, while refractory/chronic disease may involve TPO-receptor agonists, rituximab or splenectomy planning. Follow local hematology protocol.
    HEME 14 • NEUTROPENIA

    Febrile Neutropenia — a patient may be septic with almost no inflammatory response

    ANCAbsolute neutrophil countNot just total WBC
    ClockEmpiric antibacterial therapyWithin 1 hour of triage in guideline pathways
    RiskDepth + durationProfound/prolonged neutropenia = higher infection risk
    1 • Recognize

    Fever or clinical deterioration after chemotherapy/immunosuppression.

    2 • Cultures/labs

    Obtain cultures and source workup without delaying timely empiric therapy.

    3 • Antibiotics

    Broad antipseudomonal empiric coverage according to local resistance and risk pathway.

    4 • Reassess

    Perfusion, respiratory status, mucositis, line sites, skin, abdomen/perianal symptoms and organ dysfunction.

    Do not be reassured by “not looking inflamed”. Neutropenia can blunt pus, leukocytosis and local findings. Sepsis physiology wins over appearance.
    HEME 15 • SICKLE CELL

    Sickle Cell Emergencies — vaso-occlusion + hemolysis + organ risk

    Vaso-occlusive episode

    Severe ischemic pain can occur without dramatic external findings. Timely individualized analgesia and frequent reassessment matter.

    Acute chest syndrome

    New pulmonary infiltrate with respiratory symptoms/fever is a major emergency. Watch SpO₂, work of breathing, Hb drop and rapid deterioration; transfusion strategy may be required.

    Splenic / aplastic / hemolytic crises

    Acute Hb fall has different mechanisms. Pair Hb trend with reticulocytes, spleen exam/context and hemolysis markers.

    Stroke risk

    SCD is a cerebrovascular disease too; focal deficit is a stroke pathway emergency, not “just sickle pain”.

    ASH quality principle: acute vaso-occlusive pain should be assessed rapidly and pain medication delivered promptly, with reassessment every 30–60 minutes during acute management.
    HEME 16 • MASSIVE HEMORRHAGE

    MTP — hemorrhagic shock is more than “give RBC”

    RBCoxygen carriage
    Plasmacoagulation factors
    Plateletsprimary hemostasis
    Fibrinogenclot substrate
    Calciumcitrate can lower ionized Ca
    Warmthhypothermia worsens coagulopathy
    The lethal spiral: hemorrhage → hypoperfusion/acidosis + hypothermia + coagulopathy → more bleeding. Activate the institutional massive hemorrhage protocol early when indicated and trend physiology, not just unit counts.

    Nursing MTP scan

    Large-bore access • blood warmer • core temperature • ionized Ca • fibrinogen/coag trends • platelet count • source control • urine/perfusion • specimen labeling • product verification.

    HEME 17 • TRANSFUSION REASONING

    TACO vs TRALI vs Hemolysis vs Sepsis

    PatternCluesThink
    Dyspnea + hypertension + JVP/volume signsPulmonary edema after transfusion, positive balanceTACO
    Acute hypoxemia + bilateral edema without clear overloadNoncardiogenic lung injury patternTRALI
    Fever/back pain/hypotension/hemoglobinuriaEarly during RBC transfusionAcute hemolytic reaction
    High fever/rigors/shockPossible contaminated componentSeptic transfusion reaction
    Urticaria/wheeze/airway compromiseAllergic spectrumAllergic/anaphylactic
    First action is shared: stop the transfusion, assess ABC/vitals, maintain appropriate IV access and notify the blood bank/medical team. The differential comes next.
    HEME 18 • SAFETY SCAN

    Hematology Safety Scan — five questions before you act

    1 • Bleeding?

    Where, how much, active vs historical, hemodynamic effect?

    2 • Thrombosis?

    New limb swelling, chest pain, neuro deficit, line clot, organ ischemia?

    3 • Marrow / destruction?

    Retics, smear, hemolysis, pancytopenia, treatment history?

    4 • Drugs?

    Heparin, warfarin, DOAC, antiplatelet, chemotherapy, new medication?

    5 • Product?

    If transfusing: correct indication, consent/protocol, identity, baseline vitals, reaction monitoring?

    Expert habit: whenever platelets or Hb change suddenly, ask whether the patient is bleeding, clotting, destroying cells, failing production, diluting, sequestering — or whether the result is wrong.
    HEME 19 • SIMULATOR

    Hematology סימולטור קליני

    אל תבחר רק אבחנה — בחר גם את הפעולה הראשונה הנכונה.

    0/0

    HEME 20 • מבחן מסכם

    Final Hematology Exam

    15 שאלות — CBC, hemostasis, anticoagulation, emergencies, products and reactions.

    1/150/0

    פרק 8 • COMPLETE

    Hematology, Coagulation & Transfusion — complete

    Oxygen carriage

    Hb/RBC → anemia → production/loss/hemolysis.

    Primary hemostasis

    Platelets + vWF → mucosal bleeding patterns.

    Secondary hemostasis

    Coagulation factors → fibrin → PT/aPTT/fibrinogen reasoning.

    Thrombotic emergencies

    HIT and TTP are low-platelet states where thrombosis can be the dominant danger.

    Consumptive bleeding

    DIC and massive hemorrhage require trigger/source control plus targeted component support.

    Transfusion safety

    Right product, right patient, reaction recognition, stop-first response.

    Ready for Chapter 9: נוירולוגיה חריפה — seizure/status epilepticus, delirium, meningitis/encephalitis, raised ICP, spinal emergencies and neuromuscular respiratory failure.
    פרק 9 • ACUTE NEUROLOGY

    החולה “לא בסדר נוירולוגית” — מה בדיוק השתנה?

    לפני שם המחלה: timeline, consciousness, pupils, gaze, motor, language, seizure, fever, glucose and breathing.

    0%התקדמות בפרק

    מסלול פרק 9

    Neuro exam → seizures/status → altered mental status → CNS infection → ICP/herniation.

    NEURO 00 • FOUNDATIONS

    Acute Neuro Foundations — trend beats a single score

    Consciousness

    Alert? inattentive? drowsy? localizes? follows commands? Compare to baseline.

    Pupils

    Size, symmetry and reactivity. New anisocoria + deterioration is an emergency clue.

    Gaze & eyes

    Deviation, extraocular movement, nystagmus, visual fields.

    Motor

    Symmetry, drift, weakness, tone, abnormal posturing.

    Language

    Aphasia vs dysarthria vs inability to attend/participate.

    Breathing

    Airway protection, respiratory pattern, hypercapnia/hypoxemia and neuromuscular weakness.

    Neuro documentation: “GCS 13” is weaker than “newly opens eyes only to voice, confused, right arm now 2/5 from 5/5, left pupil 5 mm sluggish vs 3 mm reactive previously”.
    NEURO 01 • SEIZURES

    Seizure Academy — describe what happened before naming it

    Focal onset

    Starts in one hemisphere/network. Can be aware or impaired-awareness; motor, sensory, autonomic, cognitive or behavioral manifestations.

    Generalized onset

    Engages bilateral networks from onset; tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic and other patterns.

    During

    Protect from injury, time the seizure, support airway/oxygenation as needed; do not restrain or place objects in mouth.

    Observe

    Eyes/head, first limb involved, symmetry, automatisms, cyanosis, incontinence, duration.

    After

    Airway, glucose, vitals, neuro deficit, recovery trajectory and cause.

    Red flag

    Persistent seizure, recurrent seizures without recovery, pregnancy, trauma, infection, focal deficit or failure to wake.

    NEURO 02 • STATUS

    Status Epilepticus — the treatment clock starts at 5 minutes

    0–5 minStabilize

    Airway/oxygenation, monitor, glucose, IV/IO, focused cause search.

    5–20 minBenzodiazepine

    Adequate first-line benzodiazepine therapy per protocol.

    20–40 minSecond-line load

    Levetiracetam, valproate or fosphenytoin are established options; no single agent is clearly superior in general.

    RefractoryICU + EEG

    Escalate to continuous anesthetic/advanced therapy under neurocritical care protocol with continuous EEG.

    Common failure: repeated tiny benzodiazepine doses without adequate loading/escalation. Sedation is not the same as seizure termination; paralysis can hide convulsions while cortical seizures continue.
    NEURO 03 • NCSE

    Postictal or Nonconvulsive Status?

    Expected postictal

    Gradual improvement in attention/awareness after a convincing seizure, with no new unexplained deterioration.

    Concern for NCSE

    Failure to wake, subtle twitching/eye deviation, fluctuating unresponsiveness, unexplained aphasia/confusion or persistent coma after convulsions.

    EEG is the diagnostic bridge. A paralyzed or deeply sedated patient can still be seizing electrically. Always also search reversible causes: glucose, Na/Ca/Mg, hypoxia/hypercapnia, drugs/toxins, stroke/bleed, infection and medication withdrawal.
    NEURO 04 • DELIRIUM

    Delirium — acute brain dysfunction, not “difficult behavior”

    Core

    Acute/fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition/awareness.

    Hypoactive

    Quiet, sleepy, withdrawn — easy to miss and often mistaken for depression/fatigue.

    Hyperactive / mixed

    Agitation, hallucinations, pulling devices or fluctuating between both phenotypes.

    InfectionHypoxia / CO₂GlucoseNa/Ca/uremiaPainUrinary retentionConstipationDrugs/withdrawalSleepVision/hearing
    SCCM PADIS: structured delirium care emphasizes identifying causes and multicomponent nonpharmacologic care; evidence is insufficient to simply treat all ICU delirium with routine antipsychotics.
    NEURO 05 • CNS INFECTION

    Meningitis & Encephalitis — do not let the LP delay lifesaving treatment

    Meningitis pattern

    Fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental status; not every patient has the classic triad.

    Encephalitis pattern

    Altered behavior/mental status, seizures, focal deficits, fever; temporal-lobe features can suggest HSV but are not required.

    1 • Stabilize

    ABC, sepsis/neuro status, seizures, isolation precautions when indicated.

    2 • Cultures/labs

    Blood cultures and targeted workup without delaying empiric therapy.

    3 • CT before LP?

    Selected patients require imaging first because of mass/ICP risk; others can proceed to LP according to protocol.

    4 • Treat early

    Empiric antibacterial therapy ± dexamethasone when bacterial meningitis is suspected; IV acyclovir when HSV encephalitis is a concern, per local pathway.

    Key: if imaging/LP is delayed, appropriate empiric treatment should not be delayed while the CNS infection progresses.
    NEURO 06 • ICP

    Raised ICP & Herniation — the skull is a fixed box

    Brain

    Edema/mass increases volume.

    Blood

    Hypercapnia increases cerebral blood volume.

    CSF

    Hydrocephalus or impaired drainage increases volume.

    Warning signs: progressive GCS decline, new anisocoria/nonreactive pupil, extensor posturing, vomiting, worsening focal signs; Cushing pattern (hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing) is late and ominous.
    Position

    Head midline, HOB ~30° when appropriate; avoid neck/venous obstruction.

    Physiology

    Avoid hypoxemia, hypotension, fever and uncontrolled hypercapnia; maintain cerebral perfusion.

    Hyperosmolar

    Hypertonic saline or mannitol can reduce ICP; choice/dose depends on etiology, hemodynamics, sodium/osmolality and protocol.

    Escalate

    CSF drainage, sedation, surgery/decompression and temporary controlled hyperventilation in impending herniation according to neurocritical pathway.

    NEURO 07 • BEDSIDE

    Neuro Bedside Watch — every change has a timestamp

    Baseline + trend

    Exact time of last normal and first change.

    GCS components

    E/V/M, not only total score.

    Pupils/gaze

    Size/reactivity/asymmetry/new gaze deviation.

    Motor

    Drift, side-to-side strength, posturing.

    Airway/swallow

    Bulbar dysfunction, secretions, cough, aspiration risk.

    Metabolic

    Glucose, Na, Ca/Mg, oxygen/CO₂, temperature, renal/hepatic failure.

    Medication

    Sedatives, opioids, antiseizure drugs, withdrawal, anticoagulation.

    Escalation

    New focal deficit, seizure, GCS drop, pupil change or respiratory decline = urgent review.

    NEURO 08 • CHALLENGE

    Acute Neuro Challenge

    Generalized convulsion continues at 7 minutes.

    Status pathway: ABC/glucose + adequate benzodiazepine therapy now.

    Convulsions stopped, but patient remains unresponsive 45 minutes later with subtle eye twitching.

    Consider nonconvulsive status; EEG/escalation and cause search.

    Quiet older patient becomes inattentive and sleepy overnight after infection/urinary retention.

    Hypoactive delirium is possible; treat causes and screen rather than label “tired”.

    Fever + behavior change + focal seizure.

    Encephalitis/meningoencephalitis pathway; do not let delayed LP delay empiric treatment.

    GCS drops 14→9, left pupil becomes 6 mm fixed.

    Herniation until proven otherwise — immediate neurocritical escalation.

    NEURO 09 • SPINAL CORD

    Spinal Cord Emergency — bilateral signs demand a level

    Back/neck pain

    Especially new, severe, cancer/infection/trauma context.

    Bilateral weakness

    Quadriparesis suggests cervical level; paraparesis thoracic/lumbar cord pathways.

    Sensory level

    A horizontal dermatomal cutoff is a powerful spinal clue.

    Bowel/bladder

    Urinary retention, incontinence or constipation/obstipation can accompany cord compression.

    UMN vs early shock

    Hyperreflexia may develop later; acute severe injury can initially be flaccid/areflexic.

    Time

    Compression is a neurologic time emergency: immobilization when indicated, urgent imaging and definitive decompression/etiology treatment.

    Do not label bilateral leg weakness “deconditioning” before checking a sensory level, bladder function and spine red flags.
    NEURO 10 • CAUDA EQUINA

    Cauda Equina — roots, not spinal cord

    Cauda equina clues

    Low-back/radicular pain, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/overflow, bowel/sexual dysfunction, asymmetric lower-limb weakness and reduced reflexes.

    Why urgent

    Compression of lumbosacral roots can cause permanent bladder/bowel and motor deficits; urgent MRI and surgical evaluation are typically required.

    Bedside: ask specifically about new inability to void, reduced perineal sensation and bilateral sciatica. Patients may not volunteer these symptoms.
    NEURO 11 • SHOCK TERMS

    Spinal Shock ≠ Neurogenic Shock

    Spinal shock — neurologic

    Transient flaccidity, areflexia and loss of neurologic function below acute cord injury; reflexes can return over time.

    Neurogenic shock — hemodynamic

    Loss of sympathetic tone after high cord injury → hypotension with relative bradycardia and vasodilation; treat perfusion/hemodynamics.

    One patient can have both. Do not confuse areflexia with circulatory shock, and do not assume every hypotensive trauma patient is neurogenic — hemorrhage must be excluded.
    NEURO 12 • GBS

    Guillain-Barré — the danger is not only walking

    Pattern

    Rapidly progressive usually symmetric weakness with reduced/absent reflexes; sensory symptoms, facial/bulbar involvement can occur.

    Respiratory

    Serial FVC/VC and inspiratory pressure, cough and bulbar function matter. Pulse oximetry may remain normal until late.

    Autonomic

    Labile BP, tachy/bradyarrhythmias, ileus and urinary dysfunction can be dangerous.

    Disease-modifying therapy

    IVIG or plasma exchange are established treatments in significantly affected/rapidly worsening patients; corticosteroids alone are not effective GBS therapy.

    Respiratory riskFVC <20 mL/kgone warning threshold in guideline literature
    Trend>30% FVC fallimportant deterioration signal
    ClinicalBulbar + neck weaknesscan precede emergency intubation
    Do not wait for hypoxemia. Neuromuscular ventilatory failure is about muscle reserve and CO₂ clearance; plan airway support before exhaustion.
    NEURO 13 • MYASTHENIA

    Myasthenic Crisis — weakness can be quiet

    Typical MG physiology

    Fatigable skeletal muscle weakness: ptosis/diplopia, dysarthria/dysphagia, neck/limb weakness. Sensation is preserved.

    Crisis

    Rapid worsening with respiratory or bulbar dysfunction severe enough to threaten ventilation/airway protection.

    Trend

    FVC/VC, NIF/MIP, respiratory rate, accessory muscles and speech.

    Bulbar

    Voice, cough, secretions and swallowing — aspiration risk can be the first crisis clue.

    Triggers

    Infection, medication changes, surgery, pregnancy and drugs that worsen neuromuscular transmission.

    Rescue

    ICU airway support plus IVIG or plasma exchange; choice depends on patient factors and specialist pathway.

    A normal SpO₂ is not reassuring if the patient cannot count, cough or clear CO₂.
    NEURO 14 • RESPIRATORY LAB

    Neuromuscular Respiratory Failure — oxygenation can look fine

    Weak diaphragm→Low tidal volume→CO₂ retention→Fatigue / arrest

    FVC/VC

    Measures usable ventilatory volume and trend; falling values can warn before ABG collapse.

    NIF/MIP

    Inspiratory muscle strength. Interpretation depends on technique, cooperation and trend.

    Single breath count

    Crude bedside adjunct when formal spirometry is not immediately available; not a substitute for full assessment.

    Cough/bulbar

    Weak cough and dysphagia add airway-clearance/aspiration failure to ventilatory weakness.

    Clinical rule: If the patient is progressively weak, cannot hold head up, cannot clear secretions or respiratory measurements are falling — escalate early. Emergency intubation after exhaustion is harder and riskier.
    NEURO 15 • PHARMACOLOGY

    Acute Neuro Pharmacology — what problem is the drug solving?

    Benzodiazepine

    Rapid seizure termination; watch respiratory depression but do not undertreat true status because of fear of sedation.

    Levetiracetam / valproate / fosphenytoin

    Second-line antiseizure loading options in established status pathways; comorbidity and interactions affect selection.

    Hypertonic saline / mannitol

    Hyperosmolar therapy for ICP/cerebral edema — monitor sodium/osmolality, renal/hemodynamic context and response.

    Acyclovir

    Time-sensitive empiric HSV encephalitis coverage when clinically suspected; renal dosing/hydration and kidney monitoring matter.

    Empiric meningitis antibiotics

    Age/immunocompromise/local resistance determine regimen; do not delay for LP when unsafe/delayed.

    MG medication traps

    Some antibiotics, magnesium and other drugs can worsen neuromuscular transmission; verify medication safety in known MG.

    NEURO 16 • SIMULATOR

    Acute Neuro סימולטור קליני

    0/0

    NEURO 17 • מבחן מסכם

    Final נוירולוגיה חריפה Exam

    1/150/0

    פרק 9 • COMPLETE

    נוירולוגיה חריפה — complete

    Electrical

    Seizure → status → NCSE → EEG.

    Brain dysfunction

    Delirium/encephalopathy → reversible causes and structured assessment.

    Infection

    Meningitis/encephalitis → diagnostics must not delay treatment.

    Pressure

    ICP/herniation → pupils/GCS/perfusion/hyperosmolar escalation.

    Spine

    Sensory level + bilateral weakness + bladder = urgent cord/root thinking.

    Neuromuscular

    GBS/MG → respiratory muscle and bulbar trend before hypoxemia.

    Ready for Chapter 10: Infectious Diseases & Antimicrobial Therapy — cultures, source, empiric therapy, de-escalation, resistant organisms and infection prevention.
    פרק 10 • INFECTIOUS DISEASES

    אנטיביוטיקה היא החלטה על הסתברות — ואז עדכון לפי מידע חדש

    Host → Source → Specimen → Organism → Empiric coverage → Source control → Susceptibility → De-escalation → Duration.

    0%התקדמות בפרק

    מסלול פרק 10

    Microbiology + antibiotic reasoning + common syndromes + resistance + infection prevention.

    ID 00 • FOUNDATIONS

    Infection Foundations — organism + host + source

    Host

    Age, immune status, devices, renal/hepatic function, prior antibiotics, prior resistant organisms.

    Source

    Lung, urine, abdomen, skin, CNS, catheter, bone/joint — source determines likely organisms and penetration.

    Organism

    Gram-positive/negative, anaerobe, atypical, fungal/viral and resistance pattern.

    Severity

    Local infection vs bacteremia/sepsis/shock changes how broad and how fast empiric therapy must be.

    Colonization ≠ infection. A positive culture without compatible symptoms/source can represent colonization or contamination. Treat the patient and syndrome, not the microbiology printout alone.
    ID 01 • SPECIMENS

    Cultures — better specimen, better decision

    Blood

    Obtain appropriate sets from separate sites when bacteremia is suspected, preferably before antibiotics if this does not delay urgent treatment.

    Urine

    Culture when clinically indicated; catheter specimens require correct collection technique, not sampling from the bag.

    Respiratory

    Quality matters. Saliva contamination weakens interpretation; severe pneumonia/ventilation changes indications.

    Wound

    Superficial swabs can reflect colonizers. Deep tissue/aspirate after cleaning/debridement is often more meaningful when available.

    CSF

    Cell count, glucose/protein, Gram stain/culture/PCR as indicated; do not delay life-saving empiric therapy for unsafe/delayed LP.

    Source cultures

    Drainage fluid, joint aspirate, abscess material or device cultures can be decisive for source control.

    Diagnostic stewardship: every unnecessary culture can create a false “infection” through colonization/contamination and drive unnecessary antibiotics.
    ID 02 • ANTIBIOTICS

    Antibiotic Logic — five filters before the drug name

    1 • Coverage

    Which organisms must be covered now?

    2 • Site

    Does the drug reach lung/urine/CNS/bone/blood sufficiently?

    3 • Patient

    Allergy, kidney/liver, pregnancy, QT, interactions.

    4 • Resistance

    Prior cultures, antibiotics, hospital exposure and local antibiogram.

    5 • Toxicity

    Kidney, marrow, C. difficile, neurotoxicity, drug interactions and line burden.

    IV is not automatically “stronger”. When the patient improves, source is controlled and an effective bioavailable oral option exists, IV→PO transition can reduce line complications and burden.
    ID 03 • STEWARDSHIP

    Empiric → Targeted → Stop

    Hour 0

    Severe illness: obtain cultures rapidly and start appropriate empiric therapy.

    24–72 h

    Review cultures, imaging, source and clinical trajectory: narrow, change or stop.

    IV→PO

    Switch when improving, GI absorption works and effective oral therapy exists.

    Duration

    Use the shortest evidence-supported effective course; longer is not automatically safer.

    CDC stewardship: appropriate antibiotic use improves patient safety and limits resistance. Prospective audit/feedback and facility-specific guidance are core high-impact strategies.
    ID 04 • PNEUMONIA

    Pneumonia — syndrome first, coverage second

    CAP

    Community context and severity guide testing/site of care/empiric regimen; do not reflexively add MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage without validated risk.

    Hospital/ventilator

    Different microbiology and resistance exposure; use local hospital guideline/antibiogram.

    Aspiration

    Aspiration pneumonitis and bacterial aspiration pneumonia are not identical; history/timing and infection signs matter.

    Source control

    Empyema/complicated effusion may require drainage — antibiotics cannot drain pus.

    Respiratory deterioration can be infection, edema, PE, atelectasis or aspiration. A chest X-ray opacity is not an organism.
    ID 05 • UTI

    UTI — pyuria and bacteriuria do not equal infection

    Localized lower UTI

    Dysuria, frequency, urgency/suprapubic symptoms without systemic illness.

    Complicated / pyelonephritis

    Fever/systemic symptoms, flank pain, catheter/urologic context or sepsis; assess obstruction and source issues.

    IDSA 2025 cUTI: empiric selection should follow severity → resistance risk/prior cultures → patient factors → relevant local antibiogram in sepsis; once culture susceptibilities return, use targeted therapy and de-escalate broad coverage.
    ID 06 • SSTI

    Skin & Soft Tissue — pus needs a plan

    Cellulitis

    Diffuse skin infection without drainable abscess; identify entry point and systemic severity.

    Abscess

    Drainage/source control is often central. Antibiotics do not replace incision/drainage when indicated.

    Necrotizing infection

    Pain out of proportion, rapid progression, bullae/crepitus, toxicity or shock → immediate surgical escalation + broad empiric therapy.

    Wounds

    Colonization is common; diagnose infection by clinical tissue findings/systemic signs, not swab positivity alone.

    ID 07 • BACTEREMIA

    Bloodstream Infection — culture result + patient + source

    True bacteremia

    Compatible illness, repeated/credible culture pattern, pathogenic organism and source.

    Contamination

    Skin flora in limited bottles without syndrome can be contaminant — but devices/immunosuppression change probability.

    Source control

    Infected catheter, abscess, endocarditis, obstructed urinary/biliary source may require removal/drainage/procedure.

    Never ignore Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia as “probably contaminant”. High-risk bloodstream pathogens require directed evaluation and clearance/source strategy.
    ID 08 • C. DIFFICILE

    C. difficile — test the syndrome, not formed stool

    Risk

    Recent antibiotics, healthcare exposure, age/comorbidity and microbiome disruption.

    Diagnosis

    Clinically significant new diarrhea + appropriate stool testing. Colonization can yield positive tests without disease.

    Treatment

    IDSA/SHEA 2021 prefers fidaxomicin for many initial/recurrent adult CDI scenarios when available; oral vancomycin remains an accepted alternative in several settings.

    Prevention

    Contact precautions/environmental cleaning and antibiotic stewardship are key.

    ID 09 • AMR

    Antimicrobial Resistance — resistance history is part of the vital signs

    ESBL-E

    Extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales.

    AmpC-E

    Organisms with inducible/high-level AmpC β-lactamase risk.

    CRE

    Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales; mechanism and susceptibility guide specialist therapy.

    DTR Pseudomonas

    Difficult-to-treat resistance substantially narrows reliable antipseudomonal options.

    CRAB

    Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii — high-complexity hospital AMR.

    MRSA / VRE

    Resistant Gram-positive organisms requiring syndrome- and susceptibility-specific therapy.

    IDSA AMR Guidance 2026: prior organism, resistance mechanism, infection site and current susceptibilities matter; “broadest drug” is not a universal answer.
    ID 10 • PRECAUTIONS

    Isolation — Standard first, transmission-based on top

    Standard

    Hand hygiene, PPE by anticipated exposure, sharps/injection/device safety for every patient.

    Contact

    Gown/gloves for indicated contact-transmitted organisms; room/environment precautions.

    Droplet

    Mask on room entry for indicated droplet pathogens + source control/limited transport.

    Airborne

    AIIR when available and fit-tested N95 or higher respirator for indicated airborne pathogens.

    CDC: Contact, Droplet and Airborne precautions are added to Standard Precautions — they do not replace them.
    ID 11 • CHALLENGE

    ID אתגר יסודות

    Positive urine culture in asymptomatic catheterized patient.

    Do not equate bacteriuria with symptomatic UTI; reassess indication for catheter/culture and clinical syndrome.

    Septic shock, suspected pyelonephritis, prior ESBL urine culture 2 months ago.

    Prior susceptibility + severity + local antibiogram should influence empiric coverage.

    Blood cultures become negative, patient improves, susceptibilities show a narrow oral option.

    Reassess source, duration and de-escalation/IV-to-PO feasibility.

    Rapidly progressive leg pain with toxicity and pain out of proportion.

    Necrotizing infection until excluded: urgent surgical/source-control escalation plus antibiotics.

    New diarrhea after broad antibiotics, C. difficile positive.

    Interpret test in diarrheal syndrome; institute treatment plus appropriate contact/environment precautions.

    ID 12 • PHARMACOLOGY

    Antimicrobial Classes — learn by target and toxicity

    β-lactams

    Penicillins/cephalosporins/carbapenems: cell-wall synthesis. Time above MIC matters; allergy and renal dosing are recurring issues.

    Vancomycin

    Gram-positive/MRSA coverage in selected syndromes. Nephrotoxicity and exposure monitoring matter in serious MRSA infection.

    Macrolides

    Atypical respiratory activity among other uses; QT prolongation and interactions matter.

    Fluoroquinolones

    Excellent oral bioavailability and tissue penetration in selected infections; resistance, QT/tendon/CNS and other toxicities limit casual use.

    Aminoglycosides

    Concentration-dependent Gram-negative activity; nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity and drug-level strategy are central.

    Tetracyclines

    Doxycycline and related agents cover selected atypical, tick-borne, MRSA and other syndromes.

    Metronidazole

    Anaerobic/protozoal activity; site-specific use and interactions matter.

    Linezolid

    MRSA/VRE activity in selected syndromes; marrow suppression, serotonin interaction and neuropathy with longer exposure.

    Antifungals

    Echinocandins, azoles, amphotericin: very different spectrum, penetration, interactions and toxicity.

    Expert habit: for every antimicrobial know four things: what it covers, where it penetrates, what organ clears it, and what toxicity you are actively watching.
    ID 13 • MONITORING

    TDM & Renal Dosing — “same dose” is not same exposure

    VancomycinAUC-guidedSerious MRSA target concept 400–600 mg·h/L
    KidneyCr/eGFR trendAKI changes clearance quickly
    SafetyLevels + toxicityDrug/site-specific monitoring

    Vancomycin

    Current consensus favors AUC-guided exposure for serious invasive MRSA rather than trough 15–20 mg/L alone because of nephrotoxicity concerns.

    Aminoglycosides

    Use concentration strategy appropriate to indication; monitor renal function, concomitant nephrotoxins and ototoxicity risk.

    Renal failure

    Loading dose and maintenance interval are different questions. Dialysis/CRRT creates additional PK complexity.

    QT / marrow / liver

    Some antibiotics demand ECG, CBC or hepatic monitoring rather than kidney monitoring alone.

    ID 14 • ENDOCARDITIS

    Infective Endocarditis — bacteremia + heart structure + embolic risk

    Risk / bacteremia→Valve/device infection→Persistent bloodstream seeding→Heart failure / emboli / abscess

    Blood cultures

    When clinically stable enough, obtain multiple appropriate blood-culture sets before antibiotics; persistent bacteremia is central to the diagnostic picture.

    Imaging

    TTE/TEE and selected cardiac imaging evaluate vegetations, valve destruction, abscess and device infection.

    Complications

    Acute valve failure/HF, conduction block, stroke/systemic emboli, metastatic infection and persistent sepsis.

    Endocarditis team

    Organism-specific prolonged therapy plus early surgery/device decisions in selected complicated cases.

    2023 ESC: positive blood cultures remain a cornerstone; at least three sets are recommended before antibiotics in suspected IE when this is clinically feasible without dangerous delay.
    ID 15 • BONE & JOINT

    Bone & Joint Infection — sample deep, control source

    Septic arthritis

    Hot painful swollen joint + systemic risk → urgent joint aspiration and drainage strategy; cartilage damage is time-sensitive.

    Osteomyelitis

    Bone pain, bacteremia, wound/ulcer or spinal symptoms. MRI and bone/deep culture often matter more than superficial swab.

    Prosthetic infection

    Biofilm means antibiotics alone may fail; retention vs exchange/debridement depends on timing, organism, implant and surgical factors.

    Principle: “longer antibiotics” cannot compensate for an undrained infected joint, necrotic bone or unstable infected hardware.
    ID 16 • DEVICES

    Device Infection — biofilm changes the game

    CVC

    Assess line necessity, site, bloodstream cultures and whether line removal is part of source control.

    Urinary catheter

    Daily necessity review. Bacteriuria is common with catheters; avoid diagnosing CAUTI from culture alone.

    Cardiac devices

    Generator-pocket or lead-associated infection may require extraction rather than indefinite antibiotic suppression.

    Orthopedic prosthesis

    Biofilm + hardware stability + timing determine surgical/antibiotic strategy.

    Best infection prevention: the safest invasive device is often the one that no longer needs to be there.
    ID 17 • FUNGI

    Candidemia — Candida in blood is never “just colonization”

    Recognize risk

    Critical illness, broad antibiotics, central access, TPN, abdominal surgery, immunosuppression and others.

    Initial therapy

    Echinocandin is the standard initial concept for many adults with candidemia/invasive candidiasis.

    Clearance

    Repeat blood cultures establish bloodstream clearance; evaluate metastatic/source complications.

    Source/step-down

    Remove implicated CVC when appropriate; step down to susceptible oral azole only when clinically stable and cultures clear.

    IDSA candidiasis guideline: candidemia therapy generally continues at least 2 weeks after documented bloodstream clearance and resolution of attributable symptoms when there are no metastatic complications.
    ID 18 • ALLERGY

    Antibiotic Allergy — “penicillin allergy” needs a history

    High-risk immediate

    Anaphylaxis, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension or immediate urticaria → treat as serious allergy and select pathway accordingly.

    Low-risk / intolerance

    Nausea, headache, family history or vague childhood label may not represent IgE-mediated allergy; formal delabeling/testing can improve future antibiotic options.

    Never “test” a severe allergy informally at bedside. But also do not let an unverified label permanently force unnecessarily broad/toxic alternatives without appropriate allergy evaluation.
    ID 19 • NURSING SAFETY

    Antimicrobial Safety Scan

    Indication

    What infection are we treating? Is it documented daily?

    Specimens

    Were cultures obtained appropriately? Any result requiring narrowing?

    Organ function

    Creatinine/eGFR, liver function, dialysis/CRRT changes.

    Toxicity

    QT, CBC, renal, hepatic, neuro/ototoxicity depending drug.

    Line

    Does IV access/device remain necessary?

    Reaction

    Rash, diarrhea/CDI, anaphylaxis, infusion reaction.

    Timing

    Correct interval, infusion time and level timing.

    Stop date

    Duration and IV→PO/de-escalation reassessed.

    ID 20 • SIMULATOR

    Infectious Diseases סימולטור קליני

    0/0

    ID 21 • מבחן מסכם

    Final Infectious Diseases Exam

    1/150/0

    פרק 10 • COMPLETE

    Infectious Diseases & Antimicrobial Therapy — complete

    Diagnose syndrome

    Colonization ≠ infection; localize the source and severity.

    Sample well

    Good specimens prevent false diagnoses and support targeted therapy.

    Cover intelligently

    Host + source + prior resistance + local epidemiology determine empiric therapy.

    Control source

    Drain/remove/debride when antibiotics cannot solve anatomy.

    Narrow

    Culture/susceptibility and clinical response should reduce unnecessary spectrum/route/duration.

    Prevent

    Standard + transmission precautions, device removal and stewardship protect the next patient too.

    Ready for Chapter 11: Trauma & Acute Care — primary survey, hemorrhage, TBI/spine, chest/abdominal trauma, fractures, burns and perioperative deterioration.
    פרק 11 • TRAUMA & ACUTE CARE

    בטראומה מטפלים קודם במה שהורג קודם

    xABCDE → hemorrhage control → resuscitation → rapid localization → definitive care → reassessment.

    0%התקדמות בפרק
    ATLS 11: האלגוריתם המעודכן מדגיש xABCDE — catastrophic external hemorrhage מקבל קדימות אפילו לפני A כאשר הוא מיידי ומסכן חיים.

    מסלול פרק 11 — COMPLETE

    Primary survey → hemorrhage → organ injury → procedures → pain → complications → simulation → final exam.

    TRAUMA 00 • PRIMARY SURVEY

    xABCDE — סדר עדיפויות שמציל חיים

    המטרה אינה “לסיים בדיקה”. המטרה היא לזהות ולטפל באיום מיידי לפני שעוברים לשלב הבא.

    xeXsanguinationדימום חיצוני קטסטרופלי
    AAirway + C-spineהאם האוויר נכנס? האם הצוואר מוגן?
    BBreathingאוורור, חזה, PTX/HTX
    CCirculationפרפוזיה, דימום נסתר, דם
    DDisabilityGCS, אישונים, lateralization, glucose
    EExposureלהפשיט, לבדוק הכול, למנוע היפותרמיה
    Reassessment is part of ABCDE. שינוי בהכרה, סטורציה, דופק או לחץ דם מחזיר אותך להתחלה — לא ממשיכים אוטומטית “לשלב הבא”.
    TRAUMA 01 • HEMORRHAGE

    Hemorrhage Control — קודם לעצור את איבוד הדם

    External

    Direct pressure → wound packing/hemostatic dressing כשמתאים → tourniquet בדימום גפה מסכן חיים שאינו נשלט במהירות.

    Chest

    Hemothorax יכול להכיל נפח דם גדול. חפש ירידה בקולות נשימה + shock physiology.

    Abdomen

    דימום תוך־בטני יכול להיות סמוי. FAST/CT והמודינמיקה מכוונים את המסלול.

    Pelvis/Retroperitoneum

    שבר אגן לא יציב + shock = לחשוב bleeding source. pelvic binder מוקדם במיקום נכון יכול לצמצם נפח אגן.

    Long bones

    Femur fractures יכולים לדמם משמעותית לרקמות גם בלי דם על הרצפה.

    Shock index = HR/SBP הוא רמז, לא אבחנה. מטופל צעיר יכול לשמור BP תקין עד שאיבד נפח משמעותי.
    TRAUMA 02 • RESUSCITATION

    Damage-Control Resuscitation & Massive Transfusion

    Blood early

    ב־major hemorrhage עדיף לעבור מוקדם ל־blood-component / whole-blood strategy לפי פרוטוקול מוסדי במקום להציף crystalloids.

    TXA

    במטופל מדמם או בסיכון משמעותי לדימום: TXA צריך להינתן מוקדם ככל האפשר ובהתאם לפרוטוקול, כאשר התועלת הגדולה היא בתוך 3 שעות מהפציעה.

    Calcium + warmth

    Citrate בעירוי מסיבי מוריד ionized calcium; hypothermia + acidosis + hypocalcemia מחמירים coagulopathy.

    Lethal diamond: hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy + hypocalcemia. כאח אתה עוקב לא רק אחרי BP — גם temperature, iCa, fibrinogen/coagulation, lactate/base deficit ותגובה לעירוי.
    TRAUMA 03 • TBI

    Traumatic Brain Injury — למנוע את הפגיעה השנייה

    Primary injury

    הנזק שנגרם ברגע הטראומה: contusion, hematoma, diffuse injury.

    Secondary injury

    Hypoxia, hypotension, fever, seizures, raised ICP והפרעות גלוקוז/אוורור עלולים להחמיר מוח שכבר נפגע.

    Bedside trend

    GCS, pupils, motor asymmetry, vomiting, seizure, CSF leak, anticoagulants ומנגנון.

    Severe TBI

    BTF ממליצה לטפל ב־ICP מעל 22 mmHg כאשר מנוטר; CPP target בדרך כלל 60–70 mmHg.

    לחץ דם במוח פצוע הוא טיפול מוחי. BTF מציעה לשמור SBP ≥100 mmHg בגיל 50–69 ו־≥110 mmHg בגיל 15–49 או מעל 70, כדי להפחית secondary ischemic injury.
    TRAUMA 04 • SPINE

    Spinal Trauma — הגנה, לוקליזציה ופרפוזיה

    Neurologic injury

    חולשה/שיתוק, sensory level, paresthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction. תעד baseline לפני ואחרי העברה/פרוצדורה.

    Neurogenic shock

    פגיעת sympathetic pathways יכולה לגרום hypotension עם bradycardia/skin warm יחסית — שונה מ־hemorrhagic shock.

    אל תניח hypotension = neurogenic. בטראומה, דימום שכיח ומסוכן יותר; יש לשלול hemorrhage במקביל.
    TRAUMA 05 • CHEST

    Chest Trauma — לזהות את הדברים שלא מחכים לצילום

    Tension PTX

    Shock + respiratory distress + unilateral reduced breath sounds; אם החשד גבוה במטופל מדרדר — decompression היא החלטה קלינית דחופה.

    Open PTX

    פצע חזה מתקשר עם חלל פלאורלי; oxygen, occlusive/vented dressing לפי פרוטוקול ו־definitive chest drainage.

    Massive hemothorax

    Blood loss + reduced breath sounds; tube thoracostomy + resuscitation + surgical escalation לפי physiology/output.

    Flail / contusion

    כאב ו־pulmonary contusion פוגעים באוורור. multimodal analgesia, pulmonary hygiene וניטור respiratory failure חשובים.

    Tamponade

    Obstructive shock; FAST/echo עוזרים, אך physiology והידרדרות קובעים urgency.

    TRAUMA 06 • ABDOMEN/PELVIS

    Abdomen & Pelvis — stable vs unstable משנה הכול

    Unstable

    חפש hemorrhage source במהירות: FAST, chest/pelvis, external bleeding. אל תעכב definitive hemorrhage control בגלל CT שאינו בטוח.

    Stable

    CT עם contrast הוא כלי מרכזי להערכת solid organ/retroperitoneal injury במטופל מתאים.

    Serial exam

    כאב, guarding, distension, vitals, Hb/lactate and urine output — פגיעה חלולה יכולה להתבהר עם הזמן.

    Pelvis

    Binder over greater trochanters, לא על הבטן; הערכת דימום, GU injury ו־distal neurovascular status.

    TRAUMA 07 • ORTHOPEDICS

    Orthopedic Trauma — limb, life, function

    Neurovascular check

    Pulse, capillary refill, temperature/color, sensation, motor — לפני ואחרי splint/reduction.

    Compartment syndrome

    Pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense compartment, sensory/motor changes. Pulselessness is late.

    Open fracture

    Cover sterile, antibiotics/tetanus per protocol, alignment/splinting and urgent ortho/debridement pathway. אל “לחקור” את הפצע שוב ושוב.

    Femur/pelvis

    Long-bone/pelvic fractures are also hemorrhage problems, not רק orthopedic problems.

    TRAUMA 08 • BURNS

    Burns — airway, depth, TBSA, fluids, temperature

    Airway

    Facial burns, soot, hoarseness, enclosed-space fire or progressive edema raise concern for inhalation injury. Airway edema can worsen after arrival.

    TBSA

    Estimate partial/full-thickness burns; superficial erythema is not included in resuscitation TBSA.

    Fluids

    Formulas are starting estimates — titrate to physiology/urine output and avoid fluid creep. Large burns require structured resuscitation.

    Temperature

    Remove burned/wet material but actively prevent hypothermia.

    Burn resuscitation is not “formula = order”. It is formula → start → reassess urine output/perfusion → titrate.
    TRAUMA 09 • NURSING WATCH

    Trauma Nursing — trend, anticipate, reassess

    Airway

    Voice, secretions/blood, facial/neck injury, GCS and readiness for difficult airway.

    Breathing

    Chest movement, breath sounds, work of breathing, SpO₂/ETCO₂, chest tube function.

    Perfusion

    HR/BP are only part: skin, mental status, urine, lactate/base deficit, temperature and bleeding.

    Neuro

    GCS components + pupils + motor asymmetry, not “GCS 14” alone.

    Exposure

    Back, axillae, perineum, wounds and hidden bleeding — while preventing hypothermia.

    Reassessment

    After every intervention: did physiology improve? If not, question the diagnosis/intervention.

    TRAUMA 10 • בדיקת יסודות

    Trauma אתגר יסודות

    1/6

    TRAUMA 11 • CHEST TUBE

    Chest Tube Lab — מה המערכת מספרת לך?

    Indication

    Traumatic pneumothorax/hemothorax in selected patients, after emergent decompression when required.

    Water seal

    Tidaling may reflect pleural pressure changes. Continuous bubbling can indicate an air leak — assess patient first, then tubing/system.

    Drainage

    Trend amount/color and correlate with physiology. Sudden large bloody output or ongoing hemorrhage demands escalation.

    Never clamp casually

    Clamping a tube with an active air leak can create tension physiology. Follow indication-specific/local protocol.

    Bedside priority: if the patient deteriorates, do not spend minutes staring at the drainage box. Reassess ABC, tube position/patency, breath sounds and tension physiology.
    TRAUMA 12 • CARDIOTHORACIC

    Blunt Cardiac & Aortic Injury — mechanism matters

    Blunt cardiac injury

    Significant anterior chest mechanism can cause arrhythmia/myocardial injury. ECG and troponin are used in screening pathways; abnormal findings drive monitored evaluation.

    Blunt thoracic aortic injury

    High-energy deceleration mechanism raises suspicion. Stable patients require appropriate CT angiographic evaluation and early trauma/vascular pathway.

    Do not anchor on “chest pain = ACS”. After major trauma think pneumothorax, hemothorax, contusion, aortic injury, tamponade and cardiac injury in parallel.
    TRAUMA 13 • ABDOMINAL ORGANS

    Solid Organ & Hollow Viscus Patterns

    Spleen

    LUQ injury may bleed significantly; referred shoulder pain is possible but absence does not reassure.

    Liver

    RUQ/abdominal trauma can create large-volume hemorrhage. Hemodynamic status determines operative/interventional/nonoperative pathway.

    Kidney

    Flank mechanism/hematuria may indicate GU injury; absence of gross hematuria does not exclude all significant renal injury.

    Bowel/mesentery

    Peritonitis may evolve. Seat-belt pattern, free fluid without solid-organ injury or worsening pain/tachycardia deserve attention.

    Pancreas/duodenum

    Retroperitoneal injuries can be initially subtle and delayed.

    TRAUMA 14 • CRUSH/RHABDO

    Crush Injury & Rhabdomyolysis — muscle injury becomes systemic

    Muscle necrosis→K⁺ + myoglobin release→Arrhythmia + AKI risk→Fluids / electrolytes / renal monitoring

    Look for

    Crush mechanism, swollen painful muscle, dark urine, high CK, hyperkalemia, acidosis and rising creatinine.

    Immediate danger

    Hyperkalemia may become the first life-threatening laboratory problem; connect to the electrolyte/ECG chapter.

    Kidney

    Urine output and renal function trends matter; avoid additional nephrotoxins when possible.

    Compartment

    Rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome can coexist but are not the same diagnosis.

    TRAUMA 15 • PAIN/SEDATION

    Trauma Analgesia & Sedation — pain control without losing physiology

    Multimodal

    Acetaminophen, selected NSAID use, opioids, regional techniques and nonpharmacologic measures can reduce opioid burden when appropriate.

    Opioids

    Monitor ventilation, sedation, BP and nausea; severe pain itself worsens ventilation in rib fractures, but oversedation can hide deterioration.

    Ketamine

    Useful analgesic/sedative in selected trauma contexts, particularly when preservation of spontaneous breathing/hemodynamics is valuable; use institutional protocols.

    Reassessment

    Pain score is not enough: can the patient cough, breathe deeply, move, participate in exam and remain awake?

    ACS trauma pain guidance favors multimodal care. Pain is a physiologic problem in trauma — especially chest wall injury — not merely a comfort metric.
    TRAUMA 16 • DETERIORATION

    Perioperative / Ward Deterioration — trauma is not “over” after the OR

    Rebleeding

    New tachycardia, hypotension, drain output, Hb/lactate changes or increasing pain/distension.

    Respiratory

    Pulmonary contusion can worsen over hours; also atelectasis, PTX, PE, aspiration and opioid effect.

    Compartment

    Serial limb neurovascular checks after fixation/splinting.

    Infection

    Open wounds, contamination, devices and postoperative source issues connect to Chapter 10.

    VTE

    Trauma creates high thrombotic risk; mechanical/pharmacologic prophylaxis timing depends on bleeding/TBI/operative context.

    Delirium

    Pain, hypoxia, medications, infection, sleep disruption and older age are common contributors.

    TRAUMA 17 • PHARMACOLOGY

    Trauma Medication Clock — drug + timing + reason

    Minutes

    Analgesia, airway medications when needed, hemorrhage control adjuncts and blood products.

    <3 h

    TXA for bleeding / significant bleeding risk when indicated by trauma protocol — benefit is time-sensitive.

    Early

    Tetanus assessment and antibiotics for open fractures/contaminated injuries when indicated.

    Ongoing

    Electrolytes/calcium, analgesia, VTE prophylaxis, antimicrobial review and organ-specific medications.

    TXA is not a universal trauma drug. The 2023 European major-bleeding guideline recommends it for patients bleeding or at risk of significant bleeding as soon as possible and within 3 hours of injury.
    TRAUMA 18 • SIMULATOR

    Trauma סימולטור קליני

    אבחן את האיום שמסכן חיים עכשיו — ואז בחר את הפעולה הראשונה.

    1/100/0

    TRAUMA 19 • מבחן מסכם

    Final Trauma & Acute Care Exam

    1/150/0

    פרק 11 • COMPLETE

    Trauma & Acute Care — complete

    Prioritize

    xABCDE: fix lethal physiology before detailed diagnosis.

    Stop bleeding

    External control + source localization + blood-first damage-control resuscitation.

    Protect brain/spine

    Avoid secondary injury through oxygenation, perfusion and serial neuro exam.

    Recognize chest/abdomen

    Unstable physiology can demand treatment before perfect imaging.

    Preserve function

    Neurovascular checks, compartment surveillance, pain control and rehabilitation thinking begin early.

    Reassess

    Every intervention must change physiology — otherwise rethink the problem.

    Ready for Chapter 12: גריאטריה & Rehabilitation — frailty, falls, delirium, polypharmacy, functional decline, mobility, nutrition, pressure injury, continence and goal-oriented rehabilitation.
    פרק 12 • GERIATRICS & REHABILITATION

    בגריאטריה לא מטפלים רק במחלה — מטפלים ביכולת של האדם לחיות

    Disease + frailty + cognition + medications + nutrition + environment + goals → function.

    0%התקדמות בפרק
    ה־mental model: אדם מבוגר יכול “להחלים רפואית” ועדיין לאבד עצמאות. לכן outcome אמיתי הוא לא רק labs/vitals — אלא mobility, ADL, cognition, continence, nutrition and participation.

    מסלול פרק 12 — COMPLETE

    Frailty → CGA → falls → cognition → medications → nutrition → function → skin → continence → swallow → rehabilitation.

    GERI 00 • FOUNDATIONS

    גריאטריה — reserve matters

    Homeostasis

    Older adults may have less physiologic reserve, so a relatively small stressor can cause large functional deterioration.

    Atypical illness

    Infection, MI, dehydration or medications may present as fall, delirium, weakness or reduced intake rather than classic symptoms.

    Baseline

    Ask: What was the person doing 2 weeks ago? Walking? bathing? cooking? managing meds? Baseline is the comparator.

    Goals

    Treatment intensity should connect to what matters to the person: independence, cognition, comfort, walking, home discharge and participation.

    GERI 01 • FRAILTY

    Frailty — vulnerability, not simply age

    Lower reserve→Stress event→Disproportionate decline→Slow/incomplete recovery
    Frailty ≠ disability ≠ comorbidity. הם חופפים, אך frailty מתארת פגיעוּת מוגברת לשינוי לאחר stressor. מטופל בן 90 יכול להיות robust ומטופל בן 68 יכול להיות frail.

    Clinical Frailty Scale concept

    Judge usual baseline function before the acute illness, not how the patient looks while sick.

    Why it matters

    Frailty predicts complications, delirium, prolonged stay, institutionalization and rehab needs.

    GERI 02 • CGA

    Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment — לראות את האדם כמערכת

    Medical

    Diseases, symptoms, pain, sensory deficits.

    Medication

    Indication, burden, interactions, kidney function, adherence.

    Cognition/mood

    Delirium, dementia, depression, sleep.

    Function

    ADL/IADL, gait, transfers, falls.

    Nutrition

    Weight loss, appetite, swallowing, hydration.

    Social/environment

    Caregiver, home layout, equipment, finances, goals and discharge feasibility.

    GERI 03 • FALLS

    Falls — symptom, not diagnosis

    Screen

    Recent falls, fear/unsteadiness, gait/balance concerns.

    Assess

    Orthostatic BP, vision, feet/footwear, gait, strength, medications, cognition, environment and osteoporosis/injury risk.

    Intervene

    Exercise/strength/balance, med review, environment, vision/foot care, assistive device and individualized plan.

    CDC STEADI = Screen → Assess → Intervene. Fall prevention is multifactorial; a bed alarm alone is not a fall-prevention program.
    GERI 04 • COGNITION

    Delirium vs Dementia vs Depression

    DeliriumAcute, fluctuating, impaired attentionFind trigger: infection, meds, hypoxia, retention, pain, constipation, dehydration, sleep disruption.
    DementiaChronic progressive cognitive declineBaseline function and collateral history are essential.
    DepressionMood/anhedonia, cognitive symptoms possibleCan coexist with both dementia and delirium.
    Hypoactive delirium is easy to miss. “הוא שקט היום” יכול להיות clinical deterioration, לא שיפור.
    GERI 05 • MEDICATIONS

    Polypharmacy — indication before pill count

    Indication

    Does every drug still have a current reason?

    Benefit horizon

    Will the patient live/function long enough to benefit from preventive therapy?

    Harm

    Falls, orthostasis, delirium, bleeding, constipation, urinary retention, hypoglycemia.

    Interactions

    Drug–drug, drug–disease and renal dosing.

    Practicality

    Can the patient/caregiver actually administer this regimen?

    AGS Beers Criteria 2023 are a screening tool for potentially inappropriate medications — not an automatic “stop list”. Decisions stay individualized and person-centered.
    GERI 06 • NUTRITION

    Nutrition & Hydration — function needs fuel

    Screen

    Unintentional weight loss, intake, chewing/swallowing, dentition, depression, finances, GI symptoms and assistance needs.

    Protein/energy

    Illness and rehabilitation increase needs; preserve muscle and avoid long fasting when clinically possible.

    Hydration

    Thirst sensation may be reduced. Watch intake, sodium/urea/creatinine, orthostasis, constipation and cognition.

    Individualize

    ESPEN emphasizes comprehensive multimodal strategies rather than a supplement alone.

    GERI 07 • FUNCTION

    ADL, IADL & Mobility — למדוד מה האדם באמת עושה

    ADL

    Eating, grooming, bathing, dressing, toileting, transfers/mobility — basic self-care.

    IADL

    Medication management, finances, shopping, cooking, transport, phone/technology — community independence.

    Bed rest is an intervention with side effects. Deconditioning, orthostasis, constipation, delirium, pressure injury and loss of confidence can appear quickly. Mobilize safely and early when clinically appropriate.
    GERI 08 • SKIN

    Pressure Injury — pressure + time + vulnerability

    Risk

    Immobility, perfusion, nutrition, moisture, sensory loss, friction/shear.

    Inspect

    Skin over bony prominences and under devices; change from baseline matters.

    Offload

    Reposition individualized to tolerance/surface; heels and devices need deliberate offloading.

    Moisture

    Incontinence-associated dermatitis is not the same as pressure injury but increases skin vulnerability.

    Nutrition

    Protein/energy/hydration and wound healing are connected.

    Document

    Location, stage/category when appropriate, size/tissue/exudate/periwound and trend.

    GERI 09 • CONTINENCE

    Urinary Continence — symptom pattern first

    Urge

    Urgency/frequency; assess bladder irritants, mobility, cognition and medications.

    Stress

    Leak with cough/effort; pelvic floor factors.

    Overflow

    Retention/incomplete emptying; consider PVR, obstruction and anticholinergic/opioid effects.

    Functional

    Bladder may work, but person cannot reach/use toilet due to mobility, cognition or environment.

    Transient causes

    Delirium, infection when truly symptomatic, atrophic changes, pharmaceuticals, excess urine, restricted mobility, stool impaction.

    GERI 10 • SWALLOW

    Dysphagia — airway + nutrition + dignity

    Clues

    Cough/choke, wet voice, prolonged meals, recurrent pneumonia, weight loss, oral residue or unexplained desaturation.

    Silent aspiration

    Absence of cough does not guarantee safe swallowing.

    Oral care

    Oral bacterial burden matters to aspiration pneumonia risk; mouth care is a respiratory intervention.

    Function

    Texture, posture, assistance and adaptive equipment must preserve adequate intake and patient participation.

    GERI 11 • REHABILITATION

    Rehabilitation Reasoning — function is the treatment target

    1BaselineWhat could the person do?
    2BarrierPain? weakness? cognition? fear?
    3GoalMeaningful, measurable, patient-centered
    4PracticeRepeated task-oriented activity
    5TransferDoes ability generalize to real life?
    Rehab nursing is 24-hour rehabilitation. Transfers, toileting, dressing, medication education, sleep, pain, continence and safe independence between therapy sessions are part of treatment.
    GERI 12 • בדיקת יסודות

    גריאטריה אתגר יסודות

    1/6

    GERI 13 • PAIN

    Pain in Older Adults — pain can look like behavior

    Self-report first

    When possible, ask directly. Cognitive impairment does not automatically eliminate valid self-report.

    Nonverbal clues

    Guarding, grimacing, resistance to care, reduced mobility, sleep/appetite change or new agitation.

    Function

    Assess pain during movement and ADL — not only at rest.

    Medication risk

    Opioids, NSAIDs, sedatives and adjuvants require renal/GI/fall/delirium/constipation risk thinking.

    GERI 14 • BONE HEALTH

    Osteoporosis & Fragility Fractures

    Fragility fracture

    Low-energy fracture is a clinical clue to underlying bone fragility and future fracture risk.

    After the fracture

    Pain control, delirium prevention, early mobilization, nutrition and secondary fracture prevention belong together.

    Falls + bone

    Fall prevention without bone-health assessment misses half the problem; bone therapy without mobility work misses the other half.

    GERI 15 • BOWEL/BLADDER

    Constipation, Retention & Toileting

    Constipation

    Think immobility, low intake, opioids/anticholinergics, neurologic disease and routine disruption.

    Fecal impaction

    Can present with overflow diarrhea, urinary symptoms, pain or delirium.

    Urinary retention

    New agitation, suprapubic discomfort, low output or overflow may require bladder assessment/PVR.

    Toileting as rehab

    Scheduled access, mobility practice, clothing adaptations and environment can restore continence-related independence.

    GERI 16 • SLEEP

    Sleep — protect circadian rhythm before adding sedatives

    Daylight/activity

    Daytime mobilization and light support nighttime sleep.

    Night disruption

    Reduce unnecessary vital checks/noise when clinically safe.

    Pain/toileting

    Address symptoms that wake the patient rather than reflexively sedating.

    Medication review

    Sedative-hypnotics can worsen falls, delirium and daytime function.

    Sleep apnea

    Snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness may signal untreated sleep-disordered breathing.

    Delirium loop

    Poor sleep can worsen delirium; delirium then destroys sleep further.

    GERI 17 • SENSORY

    Vision & Hearing — sensory deprivation looks like cognition

    Hearing

    Use hearing aids, face the patient, reduce background noise, speak clearly rather than shouting.

    Vision

    Ensure glasses, lighting and contrast; poor vision raises falls risk and can worsen orientation.

    Before labeling “confused”: can the patient hear the question and see the environment?
    GERI 18 • GOALS

    Goals of Care — what are we trying to preserve?

    Understanding

    What does the patient/family understand about illness and prognosis?

    Values

    Independence? cognition? longevity? avoiding hospitalization? comfort?

    Trade-offs

    What burdens are acceptable for which benefits?

    Capacity

    Assess decision-making capacity for the specific decision; delirium can fluctuate.

    Plan

    Translate values into concrete treatment/discharge decisions and document clearly.

    GERI 19 • DISCHARGE

    Discharge Planning — discharge is a clinical intervention

    Function

    Can the patient transfer, toilet, dress, mobilize and manage stairs/home layout?

    Cognition

    Can they learn/remember instructions and recognize danger?

    Medication

    Reconcile, simplify, teach and confirm access.

    Caregiver

    Is help actually available, willing and physically able?

    Equipment

    Walker/wheelchair/commode/grab bars/bed/oxygen/wound supplies as needed.

    Follow-up

    Clear ownership, red flags and who to call.

    GERI 20 • SIMULATOR

    גריאטריה & Rehabilitation סימולטור קליני

    1/100/0

    GERI 21 • מבחן מסכם

    Final גריאטריה & Rehabilitation Exam

    1/150/0

    פרק 12 • COMPLETE

    גריאטריה & Rehabilitation — complete

    Baseline first

    Acute status is meaningless without knowing prior function/cognition.

    Frailty

    Age alone does not define reserve or recovery potential.

    Function

    ADL/IADL/mobility are clinical outcomes, not social details.

    Prevent iatrogenesis

    Bedrest, sedatives, catheters, restraints and polypharmacy can create disability.

    Rehab 24/7

    Nursing routines can either reinforce dependence or build safe independence.

    Goals

    What matters to the patient should shape treatment and discharge.

    Ready for Chapter 13: Pain & Palliative Care — pain mechanisms, opioids/adjuvants, symptom control, communication, serious-illness decisions and end-of-life nursing.
    פרק 13 • PAIN & PALLIATIVE CARE

    כאב הוא חוויה — אבל טיפול בכאב הוא reasoning

    Mechanism → intensity/function → reversible drivers → multimodal treatment → safety → reassessment → goals.

    0%התקדמות בפרק
    העיקרון: “כמה כואב?” הוא רק שאלה אחת. צריך לדעת איזה כאב, מה מחמיר/מקל, איך הוא פוגע בתפקוד, מה כבר נוסה ומה הסיכון של הטיפול.

    מסלול פרק 13 — Foundations

    Pain mechanisms → assessment → nonopioid/opioid/adjuvant therapy → toxicity → PCA → palliative principles → dyspnea → communication.

    PAIN 00 • FOUNDATIONS

    Pain Foundations — nociception is not the whole experience

    Tissue/nerve signal→Spinal processing→Brain interpretation→Pain experience→Behavior/function
    Pain is multidimensional. Sensory input interacts with attention, fear, sleep, mood, memory, meaning and context. This does not make the pain “psychological”; it explains why mechanism + person + environment all matter.
    PAIN 01 • MECHANISMS

    Nociceptive vs Neuropathic vs Nociplastic

    Nociceptive

    Tissue injury/inflammation. Somatic: localized aching/sharp; visceral: deep, diffuse, referred.

    Neuropathic

    Lesion/disease of somatosensory system: burning, electric, shooting, allodynia, paresthesia.

    Nociplastic

    Altered nociception without clear tissue damage or nerve lesion fully explaining pain; sensitization patterns can dominate.

    Why mechanism matters: the best drug for inflammatory nociceptive pain is not automatically the best drug for neuropathic pain.
    PAIN 02 • ASSESSMENT

    PQRST + Function + Safety

    P

    Provokes/palliates: movement? meal? position? touch?

    Q

    Quality: burning, pressure, cramp, electric, stabbing.

    R

    Region/radiation.

    S

    Severity — use a consistent scale when possible.

    T

    Timing, duration, breakthrough pattern.

    Function

    Sleep, breathing, walking, therapy, appetite, mood and participation.

    Reassessment: after an intervention document not only “pain now 4/10” but also sedation, respiratory status, adverse effects and whether function improved.
    PAIN 03 • MULTIMODAL

    Nonopioid & Nonpharmacologic Treatment

    Acetaminophen

    Useful component for many nociceptive pain states; check total daily exposure and liver context.

    NSAIDs

    Anti-inflammatory effect can be powerful; consider renal, GI bleeding, cardiovascular and postoperative/bone context.

    Local/regional

    Topical agents, nerve blocks/regional anesthesia and procedure-specific strategies can reduce systemic burden.

    Non-drug

    Positioning, heat/cold when appropriate, pacing, PT/OT, relaxation, sleep and education.

    CDC 2022 principle: for many common acute pain conditions nonopioid therapies are at least as effective as opioids; pain care should be multimodal and individualized. The CDC guideline does not apply to cancer, palliative or end-of-life pain.
    PAIN 04 • OPIOIDS

    Opioid Academy — analgesia and toxicity share the same receptor family

    Analgesia

    Useful for selected moderate–severe acute pain and cancer/palliative pain.

    Respiration

    Reduced respiratory drive is the most dangerous acute toxicity.

    Sedation

    Increasing sedation often precedes respiratory arrest.

    GI

    Constipation is expected with ongoing therapy and usually needs prevention.

    Patient factors

    Age, renal/hepatic function, sleep apnea, other sedatives, opioid tolerance and frailty modify risk.

    Do not confuse tolerance, physical dependence and opioid use disorder. They are different clinical concepts.
    PAIN 05 • SAFETY

    Opioid Toxicity & Naloxone — airway before score

    Increasing sedation→Slower/shallow breathing→Hypoventilation→Hypoxemia/hypercapnia→Arrest
    Response: stimulate/assess → airway/ventilation/oxygen as needed → stop opioid/sedatives → naloxone per clinical protocol when opioid toxicity is suspected → monitor for recurrence because naloxone may wear off before the opioid.
    PAIN 06 • PCA

    Patient-Controlled Analgesia — patient controlled means patient presses

    Demand dose

    The programmed bolus delivered when the patient presses.

    Lockout

    Prevents repeated doses within a defined interval.

    Basal infusion

    Not appropriate for every patient and can increase respiratory risk in opioid-naïve patients.

    PCA by proxy

    Family/staff should not press for a sleeping patient unless a specific clinician-controlled protocol applies.

    PAIN 07 • ADJUVANTS

    Adjuvant Analgesics — match drug to mechanism

    Gabapentinoids

    Neuropathic pain contexts; dizziness/sedation, renal dosing and combined opioid risk matter.

    SNRIs

    Selected neuropathic/chronic pain syndromes; BP, serotonin interactions and withdrawal considerations.

    TCAs

    Can help neuropathic pain but anticholinergic, orthostatic and cardiac effects limit use in some older adults.

    Topicals

    Lidocaine/capsaicin in selected localized neuropathic conditions can reduce systemic adverse effects.

    Corticosteroids

    Selected inflammatory, edema or cancer-related syndromes; balance glucose, infection, muscle and psychiatric effects.

    PAIN 08 • PATTERNS

    Baseline vs Breakthrough vs Incident Pain

    Baseline

    Persistent background pain requiring sustained plan.

    Breakthrough

    Transient flare despite otherwise controlled baseline pain.

    Incident

    Predictable pain with movement/procedure; pre-emptive planning may be more useful than chasing pain afterward.

    PALLIATIVE 09 • FOUNDATIONS

    Palliative Care — quality of life alongside disease treatment

    Not “giving up”

    Palliative care can be provided together with curative or life-prolonging treatment.

    Symptoms

    Pain, dyspnea, nausea, constipation, anxiety, delirium, fatigue and secretions.

    Communication

    Understanding, values, trade-offs, prognosis and what outcomes matter.

    Family/caregiver

    Support and education are part of the clinical plan.

    PALLIATIVE 10 • DYSPNEA

    Dyspnea — treat cause and perception of breathlessness

    Cause

    Fluid, infection, bronchospasm, PE, anemia, effusion, anxiety, secretions.

    Position/airflow

    Upright position and fan/airflow can reduce subjective breathlessness in selected patients.

    Oxygen

    Useful when hypoxemic; oxygen is not automatically the best treatment for every nonhypoxemic dyspnea.

    Opioids

    Low-dose opioids can be used for refractory breathlessness in appropriate palliative contexts with careful titration/monitoring.

    Anxiety

    Calm presence, explanation and targeted anxiety treatment when indicated.

    Goals

    The acceptable balance of alertness, comfort and intervention burden is patient-specific.

    PALLIATIVE 11 • COMMUNICATION

    Serious-Illness Communication — information without abandonment

    1AskWhat do you understand?
    2TellShort clear information
    3RespondAcknowledge emotion
    4ExploreWhat matters most?
    5RecommendMedical plan aligned with goals
    Communication is a clinical intervention. “Do everything” is not a goal until we understand what outcome the person is trying to achieve or avoid.
    PAIN 12 • בדיקת יסודות

    Pain & Palliative אתגר יסודות

    1/6

    PERSONAL NOTES

    מחברת קלינית

    רשום נקודות שאתה רוצה לזכור. נשמר מקומית במכשיר.

    פרק 14 • PHYSICAL ASSESSMENT / אומדן גופני

    אומדן גופני שיטתי: מה אתה רואה, מה אתה שומע, ומה זה אומר קלינית

    General survey → vitals → skin → HEENT → נשימה → לב וכלי דם → בטן → נוירו → שלד-שריר → GU/נוזלים → תיעוד והסלמה.

    0%התקדמות בפרק
    הרעיון המרכזי: אומדן גופני הוא לא רשימת V. הוא חיבור בין מראה המטופל, מספרים, ממצאי בדיקה, תפקוד ו־שינוי מה־baseline. המטרה היא לזהות יציבות מול הידרדרות, לקשר ממצא למערכת הנכונה ולדעת מתי להסלים.
    Evidence anchors: Open RN/NCBI Nursing Skills & Fundamentals; NCBI StatPearls Nursing Admission Assessment; Merck Manual bedside cardiovascular/GI examination; CDC STEADI for orthostatic BP/falls. Apply local hospital protocols for exact thresholds and documentation.

    מסלול פרק 14 — אומדן גופני

    יסודות → רושם ראשוני → vital signs → עור ופרפוזיה → HEENT → נשימה → לב → בטן → נוירו → mobility → GU/נוזלים → head-to-toe → תיעוד → challenge → simulator → final.

    PHYS 00 • FOUNDATIONS

    אומדן גופני — יסודות

    InspectPalpatePercussAuscultateInterpretActReassess

    Complete assessment

    בדיקה שיטתית ראשונית, לרוב בקבלה/שינוי מצב, כדי לקבל תמונת baseline רחבה.

    Focused assessment

    בדיקה ממוקדת לבעיה: קוצר נשימה, כאב בחזה, ירידה בהכרה, נפילה, אצירת שתן, כאב בטן ועוד.

    Trend, not snapshot

    מספר יחיד חשוב, אבל כיוון השינוי חשוב יותר: RR 18→28, HR 90→120, confusion חדשה, ירידה בתפוקת שתן.

    Function & safety

    אומדן טוב תמיד כולל: יכולת נשימה/דיבור/אכילה/מעבר/הליכה/בליעה, סכנת נפילה, aspiration או הידרדרות.
